title: Parallel Computing, Precision, and SQL
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter works through Problem Set 5 of Stat 243 (Statistical Computing), as it was assigned in three different offerings of the course (2021, 2024, 2025). Across the years the set exercises the same two skills — getting a genuinely parallel job to run correctly on a shared compute cluster, and noticing where floating-point arithmetic and query engines do something other than the "obvious" mathematical thing — plus, depending on the year, SQL querying and reading a published simulation study critically. No slides or lecture transcript were supplied for this problem set: it assumes you already have the machinery the problems draw on from earlier units — IEEE double-precision floating point, a task-parallelism library (Dask in Python, or `future`/`foreach` in R), and basic SQL — and uses the problems themselves, together with their inline hints, as the only source for this chapter. ## Running a parallel job on a shared cluster Several of the problems, across all three years, use the same setup: a job that has to read many data files, filter each one down to the rows that matter, and combine the results — in this case, one day (or one month) of Wikipedia pageview logs (date, time, language, page title, hit count, page size), filtered to the rows whose title mentions "Barack_Obama", around the 2008 US election. ### Interactive vs batch, and why files get copied to `/tmp` A short, exploratory run uses an interactive session (`srun`) with a fixed number of cores requested up front; the full-scale computation is submitted instead as a batch job (`sbatch`) that runs unattended. Both follow the same discipline: because the raw files sit on networked storage, the first step in either mode is to copy the day's files once to the local disk of the compute node (`/tmp`) before reading them — this avoids re-paying the cost of pulling the same data across the network every time the program reads it. The matching cleanup step, deleting those files from `/tmp` afterward, exists because `/tmp` is shared by whoever else is using that machine and is not reliably cleared between jobs. Because the cluster is shared, jobs also request only as many cores as the task needs — four for the single-day filtering job, up to sixteen for the month-long one (dropping to eight if the queue is backed up) — and the number of parallel workers to start is read from the scheduler's own environment variable (`SLURM_NTASKS` or `SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`) rather than hard-coded, so the same code is correct regardless of exactly how many cores a given job happened to be granted. One more piece of cluster discipline specific to Python: a batch script that spawns multiple worker processes needs its driver code wrapped in an `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard. A multiprocessing backend re-imports the script in each worker process, and without the guard that re-import would re-trigger the top-level submission logic instead of just defining functions. ### Same task, two libraries Both R's `future` (via `future_lapply`, or `foreach` with the `doFuture` backend) and Python's `dask` (via `map` or a list of delayed tasks, or `dask.bag` for the larger-scale version) are used, across the different years, for the identical task: one parallel task per input file, filtering each to the matching rows, then collecting the pieces into a single combined data frame — or, for the larger, month-long version, into a distributed data structure so that the grouping step (by day and hour) can also run across the cluster rather than only on the driving machine. For that larger version, filtering first with a `dask` bag and only afterward converting to a `dask` dataframe to do the grouping is the easier route through the tools the course had already covered. Reading the raw files has its own traps, called out explicitly for both libraries: some lines have fewer than the expected six fields, and some fields contain literal quote characters that a naive reader would otherwise treat as delimiters. In Python, `pandas.read_csv` needs the first two columns forced to string type (to keep the date/time text intact for later parsing) and its `quoting` argument set to stop it from misreading the embedded quotes; in R, `readr::read_delim()` copes with the short lines on its own, emitting a warning rather than failing. In both cases the fix is a keyword argument to the reader, not a rewrite of the filtering logic around it. The one rule that appears, stated as a hard requirement, in every year's version: test on a small subset of files — and on a single file processed serially — before running anything against the full dataset, whether that means roughly forty gigabytes compressed or a batch job that could occupy sixteen cores for half an hour. ## Floating-point arithmetic: where "obviously correct" breaks down The earlier offering of the problem set (2021) spends two problems on IEEE double-precision arithmetic itself, building on the format given in the course's own notes: $$(-1)^S \times 1.d \times 2^{e-1023}$$ with the significand $d$ held in 52 bits. ### Representable integers and the spacing near $2^{53}$ An integer $n$ with $2^{k} \le n < 2^{k+1}$ is stored as $1.d \times 2^{k}$, and specifying it exactly needs $k$ bits of the significand. As long as $k \le 52$, every integer in that range is representable exactly — which is why every integer up to $2^{53}-1$ can be stored without rounding. Once $k$ reaches 53, there are no longer enough significand bits to record every integer at that magnitude: at $2^{53}$, the spacing between numbers that can be represented exactly widens to $2$ (so $2^{53}$ and $2^{53}+2$ are both exact, but $2^{53}+1$ is not), and once the exponent increases again at $2^{54}$, the spacing doubles again to $4$. The pattern is a direct reading of the format: the significand always carries the same 52 bits of *relative* precision, so the *absolute* spacing between representable values doubles every time the exponent goes up by one. ### Accuracy lost when adding numbers of very different sizes The same limit shows up from the other direction when a computation adds numbers of very different magnitudes. A double holds a fixed number of significant decimal digits — around 15 to 16 — regardless of how large or small the number is; so once a running total has grown to order $1$, further contributions at, say, the $10^{-16}$ scale are close to or below what the format can still represent at that point. Comparing a running total built by adding many such small numbers one at a time, against calling a built-in `sum()`, is a way of seeing this directly. The hint the problem gives — that the built-in summation evidently does not simply add its inputs left to right — is itself the lesson: the accuracy of a sum in floating point depends not only on the numbers being added but on the order and the algorithm used to combine them, so a naive loop and a library function need not agree at the last few digits, and neither is simply "the exact answer." ### Denormalized numbers below the smallest normalized value Every normalized double has an implicit leading $1$ in its significand — that is what lets the format drop that bit entirely and use all 52 stored bits for the fractional part. That assumption stops holding once the exponent hits its own minimum, at $2^{-1022}$: below this smallest *normalized* value, IEEE 754 switches to *denormalized* (or subnormal) numbers, which give up the implicit leading $1$ and instead let the significand represent a value smaller than $1$. This trades relative precision for extra range near zero — the spacing between denormalized numbers does not keep shrinking in proportion to their size the way normalized spacing does — and it is why the smallest positive number a double can actually represent is very much smaller than $2^{-1022}$, rather than only just below it. ## SQL: writing one query several ways, and knowing they agree The two later offerings (2024, 2025) replace the floating-point problems with a SQL exercise against a Stack Overflow database: find every user (with display name) who has asked a question but never answered one. ### Four constructs, one answer The same question can be phrased with any of several SQL constructs — a subquery inside a `WHERE` clause (e.g. excluding users whose id appears among answerers), a subquery inside a `FROM` clause (building an intermediate table first), a set operation (`INTERSECT`, `UNION`, or `EXCEPT` between the set of askers and the set of answerers), or an outer join with a `NULL` check on the non-matching side. Because all four describe the same set of users, checking that they return the same *count* is itself the check that the four formulations are logically equivalent — a query that looks right but returns a different count than the others has a bug. One SQLite-specific wrinkle: the engine has no right outer join, so an outer-join formulation needs the "asked" table on the left, not written the way the English sentence might first suggest. A wrinkle worth carrying into any real dataset: a join or filter key that contains `NULL`s behaves differently from one that does not, because `NULL` never satisfies an equality comparison — a row with a `NULL` owner id silently disappears from a join on that column rather than raising an error. Where this matters, building a view that first drops the offending `NULL` rows keeps that data-cleaning step separate from, and out of the way of, the logic answering the actual question. ### The same answer, different costs Logically equivalent queries need not cost the same to run, and the exercise's second half asks for exactly that comparison: timing the different formulations against each other, and the same query against two different database engines (SQLite and DuckDB). Getting the same answer four different ways is the correctness check; timing them is the reminder that "correct" and "equally efficient" are different questions. ## Reading a simulation study, not just a method The 2021 offering also assigns a critical reading of a published simulation study — Cao et al. (2015), in the *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B* — with the method itself, an estimating-equation-based regression for time-varying covariates, deliberately treated as a black box: solving its estimating equation for $\hat\beta$ plays the same role that differentiating a sum-of-squares criterion and setting it to zero plays in ordinary regression, and the kernel it uses simply downweights observation-covariate pairs that were measured far apart in time. The exercise is about the simulation study that supports the method, not the method's derivation, and it structures that reading around three questions that generalize to any simulation study: - What is the study trying to establish, and what metric or metrics does it use to establish it? - What choices did the authors have to make in setting up the data-generating mechanism, and which of those choices could plausibly change how favorably the method comes out? - Looking at the paper's own results tables, what would the numbers need to look like, concretely, for the method to count as a good one? ## Exercises 1. **Floating-point spacing near $2^{53}$.** Demonstrate that the integers $1, 2, \dots, 2^{53}-1$ can each be stored exactly in the double format $(-1)^S \times 1.d \times 2^{e-1023}$ — a few examples showing the pattern are enough; you do not need to write $e$ in binary. Then show that $2^{53}$ and $2^{53}+2$ can still be represented exactly but $2^{53}+1$ cannot, so the spacing between representable numbers near $2^{53}$ is $2$, and that from $2^{54}$ onward the spacing between representable integers is $4$. Confirm the pattern by evaluating $2^{53}-1$, $2^{53}$, and $2^{53}+1$ directly in R. 2. **Summation of numbers with very different magnitudes.** Consider the sum of $1$ and ten thousand copies of $10^{-16}$; mathematically this is $1 + 10^{-12} = 1.000000000001$. a. Before doing any computation: how many digits of this result can a double actually be expected to hold? b. Form the length-$10001$ vector $x = (1, 10^{-16}, \dots, 10^{-16})$ in R and check whether `sum(x)` achieves the accuracy you expected in (a). c. Repeat in Python (`numpy`, printing extra digits with `decimal.Decimal`). d. Sum the vector with an explicit loop, $((x_1+x_2)+x_3)+\cdots$, once with the $1$ placed first and once with it placed last. Compare the loop's accuracy to `sum()`'s, and to each other, in both R and Python. 3. **Parallel filtering of a single day of Wikipedia traffic.** One day of Wikipedia pageview logs (date, time, language, page title, hit count, page size) sits on a shared cluster's network storage. On an interactive four-core session, using a task-parallel library (Dask in Python, or `future`/`foreach` in R): a. copy that day's files to the local `/tmp` of the compute node; b. read and filter them in parallel to the rows whose page title mentions "Barack_Obama", collecting the matches into a single data frame; c. tabulate hits by hour and plot how traffic varied over the day (the timestamps are UTC, so this one day's plot will not show the U.S. evening); d. remove the copied files from `/tmp`. Test on a small subset of files, and on one file processed serially, before running the parallel version on the full day. Then repeat steps (a)-(b) as a batch job submitted to the cluster's scheduler instead of an interactive session, guarding the driver code so a multi-process backend does not re-trigger job submission when it re-imports the script. 4. **Parallel filtering and grouping over a month.** Repeat the filtering of Exercise 3 over a full month of the same Wikipedia data (about 40 GB compressed, already staged on the cluster so it does not need to be copied per student), using a distributed data structure so that both the filtering and the grouping by day and hour run across the cluster. Time the parallel part of the computation. Once you have hourly counts for the whole month, plot the traffic trend across the month and, in more detail, across election day and the day after (November 3-5, 2008 — the result was declared at 11pm Eastern on November 4). Keep the number of cores requested within whatever limit the class agreed to share, and read the number of workers to start from the scheduler's own environment variable rather than hard-coding it. 5. **SQL on the Stack Overflow database.** Find every user (with display name) who has asked a question but never answered one. First build views that drop the rows in the relevant tables where the owner id is `NULL`. Then write enough separate queries against those views to demonstrate, between them: a subquery in a `WHERE` clause, a subquery in a `FROM` clause, a set operation (`INTERSECT`, `UNION`, or `EXCEPT`), and an outer join (SQLite has no right outer join, so think about which table needs to be on which side). Check that all your queries return the same count of users. Then compare how long the different formulations take to run, and whether that changes between two different database engines. 6. **Reading a simulation study.** Read the introduction, the data-generating setup, and the simulation results of a published paper proposing an estimating-equation method for a regression problem with time-varying covariates (treat the estimation procedure itself as a black box: its estimating equation plays the role that setting the derivative of a sum of squares to zero plays in ordinary regression, and its kernel simply downweights covariate-response pairs measured far apart in time). In a few sentences each: a. What is the simulation study trying to show, and what metrics does it use to show it? b. What choices did the authors have to make in setting up the data-generating mechanism, and which of those choices could plausibly change how favorably the method comes out? c. Looking at the paper's results tables, what would you want to see, numerically, for the method to count as a good one? 7. **Extra credit: the smallest representable positive number.** a. Find, experimentally, the smallest positive number your language's floating-point format can represent, and give its value in base 10. (It is considerably smaller than $10^{-308}$.) b. The smallest *normalized* double is $2^{-1022}$. Explain how a smaller positive number can be represented at all. Start from the bit pattern of $2^{-1022}$ and work out what the bit pattern one step below it actually represents — you should recognize the resulting number. Continue the pattern down to the smallest representable positive value, and give it in both base 2 and base 10. ## Sources - Comments and problem statements: `berkeley-stat243/fall-2024/ps/ps5.qmd`, split in the library as [`01-comments.md`](https://github.com/berkeley-stat243/fall-2024/blob/9c62305d05fca31df0d9c6a3b68b350ad8722fee/ps/ps5.qmd) and [`02-problems.md`](https://github.com/berkeley-stat243/fall-2024/blob/9c62305d05fca31df0d9c6a3b68b350ad8722fee/ps/ps5.qmd), licensed CC BY 4.0 — source of the Dask/cluster and SQL exercises (Exercises 3-5) and the shared cluster etiquette above. - `berkeley-stat243/fall-2025/ps/ps5.qmd` ([ps5.md](https://github.com/berkeley-stat243/fall-2025/blob/035a19ebd7ab88cffca907cade6d40212d575a1f/ps/ps5.qmd)), licensed CC BY 4.0 — the near-identical restatement of the same Dask and SQL exercises the year after, used to confirm which details (core limits, environment variables) are stable across offerings. - `berkeley-stat243/stat243-fall-2021/ps/ps5.pdf` ([ps5.md](https://github.com/berkeley-stat243/stat243-fall-2021/blob/c918dcc56a197cc539e270f1f7d076010b175c52/ps/ps5.pdf)), licensed CC0-1.0 — source of the floating-point exercises (Exercises 1, 2, 7), the R/`future` version of the parallel-filtering exercise, and the simulation-study exercise (Exercise 6).
